30353:
Mary Magdalene came from Magdala, a fishing town on the Sea of Galilee. Luke says Jesus had freed her from seven demons, and that she and other women travelled with Jesus and the Twelve, supporting them financially. She is named in all four Gospels at the crucifixion, at the burial, and at the empty tomb, usually first among the women, which suggests she was prominent among Jesus' followers.

In John's Gospel she is the first person to see the risen Jesus and is sent to tell the disciples, which led early writers to call her 'apostle to the apostles'. Nothing in the New Testament says she was a prostitute or married to Jesus. The 'penitent prostitute' image arose in the West when Pope Gregory the Great (591) merged her with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary of Bethany; Eastern churches never made this identification, and the Catholic Church quietly separated them in its 1969 calendar reform.

Recent interest, fuelled by Gnostic texts such as the Gospel of Mary and the Gospel of Philip and by popular fiction, has made her a focus of debates about women's leadership in early Christianity.
30354: She was healed of seven demons (Luke 8:2; Mark 16:9), supported Jesus' ministry (Luke 8:3), followed from Galilee and watched the crucifixion (Mark 15:40-41), saw the burial (Mark 15:47), came to the tomb (Matt 28:1; Mark 16:1; Luke 24:10; John 20:1), and was the first to see the risen Jesus according to John 20:14-18 and Mark 16:9 (the longer ending, absent from the earliest manuscripts).
30356: Following Gregory the Great (Homily 33 on the Gospels), she was identified with the sinful woman who anointed Jesus (Luke 7:36-50) and with Mary of Bethany, becoming the great model of the repentant sinner. This view shaped centuries of art and devotion.
30357: Always distinguished her from the sinful woman and Mary of Bethany; she is honoured as a Myrrh-bearer and 'Equal-to-the-Apostles' for proclaiming the resurrection.
30359: Most now reject the conflation as unsupported by the text. In 2016 the Catholic Church raised her memorial to a feast, calling her 'apostle of the apostles'. Protestants emphasize her as the first resurrection witness and a model of devoted discipleship.
30361: Sees her as a leading disciple whose role was minimized in later tradition; Gnostic texts reflect 2nd-century debates over her authority versus Peter's. Claims that she was Jesus' wife have no early evidence; the Gospel of Philip's 'companion' passage is fragmentary and late.
30363: Courageous loyalty at the cross and tomb (Mark 15:40-47)
30365: Initially assumes the body has been stolen (John 20:2; John 20:13)
30367: Hearing her name at the tomb (John 20:16)
30368: Magdala (Migdal), excavated since 2009, had a 1st-century synagogue and a fish-processing industry. Women travelling with a teacher and funding him was unusual but not unheard of among well-off women; Joanna, wife of Herod's steward Chuza, was among them (Luke 8:3). The testimony of women carried less legal weight in Jewish and Roman settings, which many historians see as a sign that the women-at-the-tomb tradition was not invented.
30369: Mary Magdalene is one of the most depicted saints in Western art, usually with an ointment jar and long hair. The English word 'maudlin' derives from the tearful penitent of later legend. Her feast is 22 July.
30370: She was conflated with the sinful woman of Luke 7 and with Mary of Bethany.
30372: She went with the apostle John and Mary to Ephesus, where she died and was buried.

30374: She sailed to Provence with Lazarus and Martha, preached at Marseille and spent her last years as a hermit at Sainte-Baume.

30376: She was called 'apostle to the apostles'.
30377: Hippolytus, Commentary on the Song of Songs 25 (needs-verification); Thomas Aquinas, Commentary on John 20
30378: Intense, grieving and devoted; speaks from deep personal gratitude and with the urgency of someone who has seen something no one will believe.

30394: Martha, sister of Mary and Lazarus of Bethany near Jerusalem, appears as an energetic host who welcomed Jesus into her home. Luke's story of her frustration with her contemplative sister has made 'Martha and Mary' a classic image of active and contemplative lives. John gives her a weightier role: after her brother's death she makes one of the Gospel's clearest confessions of faith, parallel to Peter's. John notes simply that Jesus loved Martha, her sister and Lazarus.
30395: Luke calls the house hers (Luke 10:38). John records that Jesus loved her (John 11:5) and her confession 'You are the Christ, the Son of God, who is coming into the world' (John 11:27).
30396: Martha and Mary symbolize the active and contemplative lives, both honourable, with contemplation as the 'better part'. Orthodox count her among the myrrh-bearers.

30398: She went to Provence and tamed a dragon (the Tarasque) at Tarascon.

30407: She listens to his teaching as a disciple would, and Jesus defends her choice.

30411: She pours a pound of costly nard on Jesus' feet and wipes them with her hair; Jesus says she has kept it for his burial. Mark and Matthew tell of an unnamed woman anointing his head at Bethany, usually identified with her.
30412: Mary, sister of Martha and Lazarus, is consistently pictured at Jesus' feet: listening as a disciple, grieving after her brother's death, and pouring expensive perfume on him days before his crucifixion. Jesus said her act of devotion would be told wherever the gospel is preached. Western tradition later merged her with Mary Magdalene and with the sinful woman of Luke 7, an identification most interpreters now reject.
30413: She sat at the Lord's feet listening (Luke 10:39), was loved by Jesus (John 11:5), and anointed him six days before Passover (John 12:1-3).
30415: Identified with Mary Magdalene and the sinful woman of Luke 7 (Gregory the Great), a model of penitence and contemplation.
30417: A distinct person; her anointing in John 12 is seen as a prophetic act preparing Jesus for burial and possibly as a royal anointing.

30424: His sisters send word: 'He whom you love is ill.' Jesus delays two days, saying the illness is for God's glory.

30431: Lazarus lived in Bethany, near Jerusalem, with his sisters Martha and Mary, and is described as a friend whom Jesus loved. His raising after four days in the tomb is the seventh and climactic sign in John's Gospel and, in John's narrative, the event that triggers the decision to have Jesus killed. Lazarus never speaks in the text. He is different from the poor man Lazarus in Jesus' parable (Luke 16:19-31), though the shared name has invited comparison.
30432: John 11:3, John 11:5 and John 11:11 call him the one Jesus loves and 'our friend'. He had been in the tomb four days (John 11:17; John 11:39).
30434: A sign pointing to Jesus as 'the resurrection and the life' and anticipating his own resurrection; Lazarus returns to mortal life, whereas Jesus rises to immortal life.

30436: He fled persecution to Cyprus, became bishop of Kition (Larnaca), and died there; his tomb lies beneath the Church of Saint Lazarus.

30440: A man who has passed through death: quiet, grave and grateful, with little need to argue.
30444: Member of the Sanhedrin ('ruler of the Jews')
30448: Knowledge of the Law and procedure

30453: When the Pharisees condemn Jesus, he asks whether the Law judges a man without hearing him; they mock him as a Galilean sympathizer.
30455: With Joseph of Arimathea he brings about seventy-five pounds of myrrh and aloes, a royal quantity, to prepare Jesus' body.
30456: Nicodemus was a Pharisee and member of the Jewish ruling council in Jerusalem who came to Jesus at night, puzzled by his teaching on new birth. John's Gospel follows him through three scenes: from tentative seeker, to cautious defender of fair procedure in the council, to open participant in Jesus' burial with an extravagant amount of spices. Whether he became a full believer the text leaves the reader to judge.
30457: He is 'a man of the Pharisees', 'a ruler of the Jews' (John 3:1) and 'the teacher of Israel' (John 3:10). John repeatedly notes that he first came by night (John 19:39).
30458: Venerated as a saint and myrrh-bearer who became a disciple; John 3 is read in connection with baptism ('born of water and the Spirit').
30460: The classic example of a religious man needing to be 'born again' through personal faith; his progression shows faith growing from secret to public.
30461: A literary figure representing sympathetic Jewish leaders whose faith remained inadequate or hidden; his role in the burial is read by some as honouring Jesus as king, by others as treating him as definitively dead.
30462: The apocryphal Gospel of Nicodemus (Acts of Pilate), 4th century, bears his name and narrates Jesus' trial and descent into hell.
30463: Gospel of Nicodemus / Acts of Pilate
30464: Learned, careful and courteous, asking literal-minded questions; a man of position who weighs every step.
30466: 'May he add'; Arimathea is usually identified with Ramathaim (Ramah)
30473: A good and righteous man, he had not consented to the council's decision.
30475: He takes courage to approach Pilate, who grants the body after confirming Jesus is dead.
30476: Buries Jesus in his own new tomb
30477: With Nicodemus he wraps the body in linen and lays it in a new rock-cut tomb in a garden near the place of crucifixion, rolling a stone across the entrance.
30478: Joseph of Arimathea was a wealthy, respected member of the Jewish council who, all four Gospels agree, took responsibility for Jesus' burial. He was waiting for the kingdom of God, had opposed the council's verdict and was a secret disciple for fear of the authorities. By asking Pilate for the body of an executed rebel he took a public risk, and by placing it in his own new tomb he provided the setting for the empty-tomb narratives. Many historians consider the burial tradition early and reliable precisely because Joseph was a council member, an unlikely invention.
30479: He was rich (Matt 27:57), a respected council member (Mark 15:43), a disciple secretly (John 19:38) and had not agreed with the council's action (Luke 23:51).
30480: Fulfils Isa 53:9, the servant 'with the rich in his death', and shows that faith hidden by fear can come into the open at the decisive moment.
30481: Most accept a burial by a Jewish council member as historical; a minority (e.g. Crossan) doubt it, arguing crucified bodies were often left or put in common graves, while others point to Josephus and the Giv'at ha-Mivtar ossuary showing that crucified Jews could be buried.
30482: He brought the Holy Grail to Britain and founded the church at Glastonbury.
30483: Robert de Boron, Joseph d'Arimathie (c. 1200); later Glastonbury traditions
30484: He was imprisoned by the Jewish leaders and miraculously freed by the risen Jesus.
30486: Dignified and discreet, a man of standing who chooses his words carefully but acts decisively when it matters.
30492: Climbs a sycamore to see Jesus
30493: Too short to see over the crowd, he climbs a sycamore-fig; Jesus invites himself to his house. Zacchaeus gives half his goods to the poor and repays fourfold anyone he has defrauded, and Jesus declares that salvation has come to his house.
30494: Zacchaeus was a rich chief tax collector at Jericho, a key customs point on the road to Jerusalem. His encounter with Jesus on the final journey to Jerusalem is told only in Luke, which closes with Jesus' mission statement: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. His restitution goes beyond what the Law required (compare Exod 22:1; Lev 6:5).
30495: Luke 19:2-3 says he was a chief tax collector, rich and small in stature.
30496: Peter appointed him the first bishop of Caesarea.
30498: Eager and impulsive, a little defensive about his reputation, then overflowing with generous resolutions.
30507: Mixes Galileans' blood with their sacrifices
30508: Jesus is told of Galileans Pilate had killed while they were sacrificing, an incident otherwise unknown but consistent with his reputation.
30510: He questions Jesus about being King of the Jews, finds no basis for a charge, sends him to Herod Antipas, offers to release him or Barabbas, washes his hands (Matt 27:24) and finally hands him over to be crucified under pressure from the crowd and the threat of being 'no friend of Caesar'.

30515: Pontius Pilate was the Roman prefect (governor) of Judea from AD 26 to 36, an equestrian administrator based at Caesarea Maritima who came to Jerusalem at festivals to keep order. He is the official who sentenced Jesus to crucifixion, which is why his name is recited in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds. The Gospels show him as reluctant and convinced of Jesus' innocence but yielding to pressure; Philo and Josephus describe him as stubborn, provocative and harsh. A 1961 inscription at Caesarea confirms his name and title. He was recalled to Rome after a violent suppression of Samaritans in 36.
30516: The Gospels portray him asking 'What is truth?' (John 18:38), declaring Jesus innocent (Luke 23:4; John 19:4), and handing him over to satisfy the crowd (Mark 15:15). His wife sends warning of a dream (Matt 27:19). Acts and 1 Tim 6:13 remember the trial before him.
30518: Venerate Pilate (and his wife Procla) as saints, following traditions that he became a believer.
30520: A weak, compromised judge whose hand-washing could not remove guilt; named in the creed to anchor the gospel in history.
30521: Many think the Gospels soften Pilate's role to reassure Roman readers, given Philo's and Josephus' portrait; others argue a politically cautious governor would plausibly avoid a riot at Passover.
30522: Josephus (Antiquities 18.55-62, 18.85-89) records Pilate's bringing military standards with images into Jerusalem, using temple funds for an aqueduct, and massacring Samaritans; Philo (Embassy to Gaius 299-305) describes golden shields offensive to Jews and calls him inflexible and cruel. Tacitus (Annals 15.44) notes that Christ suffered the extreme penalty under Pontius Pilate.
30523: Pilate fell into misfortune under Caligula and took his own life.
30525: His wife, named Procla or Claudia Procula, became a Christian.
30526: Gospel of Nicodemus 2; Origen, Homilies on Matthew (needs-verification)
30527: Clipped, sardonic and wary; a Roman official balancing contempt for local quarrels with fear for his own position.
30528: Family name, meaning uncertain; his personal name was Joseph (Josephus)
30537: After Lazarus is raised, he argues it is expedient for one man to die for the people rather than the nation perish; John reads this as an unintended prophecy.
30539: Chief priests and elders gather in his palace to arrest Jesus by stealth.
30541: After false witnesses fail to agree, he asks Jesus under oath whether he is the Christ; at Jesus' answer about the Son of Man he tears his robes and declares blasphemy.
30543: With Annas he questions Peter and John and orders them not to teach in Jesus' name.
30544: Joseph Caiaphas was high priest from about AD 18 to 36, an unusually long tenure that suggests skilful cooperation with Roman prefects, including Pilate, who was removed at about the same time. Son-in-law of the former high priest Annas, he presided over the council that condemned Jesus and handed him to Pilate, reasoning that one man's death was better than Roman reprisal against the nation. An ornate ossuary inscribed 'Joseph son of Caiaphas', found in Jerusalem in 1990, may belong to him, though the identification is debated.
30545: He was high priest 'that year' and son-in-law of Annas (John 11:49; John 18:13). He interrogated Jesus and charged him with blasphemy (Matt 26:63-66).
30547: The chief human agent of Jesus' condemnation, often used as a symbol of religious power protecting itself. Modern churches stress that he does not represent 'the Jews' collectively (Nostra Aetate, 1965).
30548: A pragmatic aristocrat responsible for order at Passover under Roman oversight; executing a messianic claimant who disturbed the temple would fit that role.
30549: Josephus (Antiquities 18.35, 18.95) records his appointment by Valerius Gratus and removal by Vitellius. The high priest controlled the temple and its treasury and was the main Jewish intermediary with Rome.
30550: Smooth, calculating and authoritative; frames ruthless decisions as prudent statesmanship.
30559: Jesus is brought first to Annas, who questions him about his disciples and teaching before sending him bound to Caiaphas.
30561: Named first among the high-priestly family examining Peter and John.
30562: Annas was high priest from AD 6 to 15, appointed by the Roman legate Quirinius and deposed by Valerius Gratus. He remained the power behind the office: five of his sons and his son-in-law Caiaphas also served as high priest. Luke speaks of 'the high priesthood of Annas and Caiaphas' (Luke 3:2), reflecting his continuing status, and John has Jesus examined by him first.
30563: He is father-in-law of Caiaphas (John 18:13) and is still called high priest in Acts 4:6.

30565: An elder statesman of the priesthood: patient, probing and accustomed to deference.

30587: Herod the Great ruled Judea as a Roman client king from 37 to 4 BC. An Idumean whose family had converted to Judaism, he gained power through Roman patrons (Mark Antony, then Augustus) and kept it through skill and brutality, executing a wife (Mariamne) and three sons. He was also one of antiquity's great builders: he rebuilt and vastly expanded the Jerusalem temple, and built Caesarea Maritima, Masada, the Herodium and palaces at Jericho. Matthew's account of his slaughter of Bethlehem's infants is not recorded elsewhere, but fits his paranoid character in Josephus. His death date, usually 4 BC, is the main anchor for dating Jesus' birth.
30588: Matthew presents him as a ruler who sought to destroy the newborn king (Matt 2:13) and died soon after (Matt 2:19). John 2:20 says the temple had been under construction for forty-six years.
30590: Matthew portrays Herod as a new Pharaoh and Jesus as a new Moses rescued from a king's massacre (Exod 1:22); the Holy Innocents are honoured as martyrs (28 December in the West).
30591: Some doubt the massacre's historicity because Josephus omits it; others note that Bethlehem's infant population would have been small (perhaps a dozen or two) and that Josephus did not record every atrocity.
30592: Josephus, Antiquities books 14-17 and Jewish War book 1, is the main source. Herod died at Jericho after a painful illness and was buried at the Herodium, where archaeologist Ehud Netzer identified his probable tomb in 2007. His kingdom was divided among Archelaus, Antipas and Philip.
30593: Charming and grandiose in public, suspicious and menacing in private; speaks as a man who trusts no one.
